MSK–Skin · Week 15 · Lecture Companion

Anterior Forearm and Elbow

Dr. Shannon Barwick · Anatomy · Course-first learning with selective board connections

Orientation

Learning objectives & big picture

  1. Identify distal humerus, radius and ulna landmarks, articulations and ligaments; explain injuries and elbow instability.
  2. Organize anterior and posterior forearm compartments, muscle layers and neurovascular supply.
  3. Explain anterior forearm muscle attachments, action, innervation and tests.
  4. Trace median and ulnar nerve pathways and predict injury findings.
  5. Trace radial/ulnar vessels, superficial veins, lymphatics, collateral networks and pulse sites.
  6. Explain pronator syndrome and cubital tunnel syndrome clinically.
  7. Recognize relevant structures in X-rays, MRI and CT.
BIG PICTURE

The anterior forearm is mainly a flexor–pronator compartment. The median nerve supplies most muscles, but the flexor carpi ulnaris and medial (4th/5th digit) flexor digitorum profundus belong to the ulnar nerve. Linking attachments → motion → nerve → lesion is the fastest way to localize deficits.

Objective 1

Bony landmarks, articulations & injury

Radius versus ulna

Radius: lateral, shorter; radial head/neck, radial tuberosity and styloid process. Ulna: medial, longer; olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear/radial notches and distal head/styloid. The ulna does not directly articulate with the carpal bones at the wrist. The interosseous membrane is a fibrous radioulnar syndesmosis that stabilizes both bones and has openings for vessels.

Distal humerus

Capitulum meets radial head; trochlea meets the ulnar trochlear notch. Anterior radial and coronoid fossae accommodate those processes during flexion; posterior olecranon fossa accommodates the olecranon during extension.

Three stabilizing ligament systems

  • Annular ligament: ring around radial head; stabilizes the proximal radioulnar pivot joint.
  • Radial collateral ligament: fans from lateral epicondyle and blends with annular ligament.
  • Ulnar collateral ligament: triangular structure on medial side of elbow.
  • TFCC: stabilizes distal radioulnar relationship (ulnar head against radial ulnar notch).
CLINICAL CONNECTION

Colles fracture: distal radius after a fall on an outstretched, dorsiflexed hand (FOOSH). Nursemaid’s elbow: sudden traction on a pronated arm in a child can sublux the radial head relative to annular ligament. Elbow dislocation can threaten stabilizing ligaments and nearby neurovascular structures; this latter injury relationship is an additional clinical inference, not described in detail in these slides.

Retrieval checkpoint · Which humeral surface articulates with the radial head, and which ligament encircles it?

Capitulum; annular ligament.

Objective 2

Layers and functional compartments

Antebrachial fascia encloses forearm musculature; the interosseous membrane separates radius and ulna. Anterior muscle groups mainly flex/pronate; posterior mainly extend/supinate. The anterior group is presented as 4 superficial + 1 intermediate + 3 deep.

LayerMusclesMain innervation
Superficial (4)Pronator teres (PT), flexor carpi radialis (FCR), palmaris longus (PL), flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU)Median except FCU (ulnar)
Intermediate (1)Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS)Median
Deep (3)Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP), flexor pollicis longus (FPL), pronator quadratus (PQ)Median/anterior interosseous except medial FDP (ulnar)
MUST KNOW Anterior compartment nerve rule: median except FCU and ulnar half of FDP. The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is a median branch supplying FPL, PQ, and lateral FDP.
Retrieval checkpoint · An ulnar neuropathy at the elbow weakens which two anterior-forearm motor groups?

Flexor carpi ulnaris and medial FDP (flexion of distal phalanges of digits 4 and 5).

Objective 3

Anterior forearm muscles: learn by movement

The professor gives explicit attachments, nerve roots and actions on slides 17–30; the functional bedside tests below are anatomical applications (the slides do not specify formal examination maneuvers). The four superficial muscles share the medial epicondyle/common flexor origin although PT and FCU have additional ulnar heads.

MECHANISM → EXAM FINDING

FDS inserts on middle phalanges → primarily bends PIP. FDP inserts on distal phalanges → bends DIP. FPL inserts at distal phalanx of thumb → flexes thumb IP joint. When a patient cannot form a normal tip-to-tip “OK” sign, consider weakness of AIN-innervated FPL and lateral FDP.

COURSE DETAIL The slide calls medial epicondyle overuse “Median Epicondylitis”; the usual clinical term is medial epicondylitis (golfer’s elbow). It involves the common flexor tendon after repeated wrist flexion; this correction is explicitly identified rather than silently altered.
Retrieval checkpoint · A patient has intact PIP flexion but impaired DIP flexion of the index finger. Which muscle and nerve branch?

Lateral FDP; anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.

Objectives 4 and 6

Nerve pathways, lesions & compression syndromes

Median nerve

Receives contributions from lateral and medial cords (C5–T1 on course slide). Enters elbow near brachial artery; passes through the anterior forearm and between heads of pronator teres. Supplies almost all anterior forearm muscles. Branches into AIN for PQ, FPL and lateral FDP. Distal compression under flexor retinaculum produces carpal tunnel syndrome (mentioned for differentiation).

Ulnar nerve

Origin listed as medial cord (C7–T1 on course slide); passes posterior to medial epicondyle and between/under proximal FCU heads (elbow relation is clinical enrichment). In forearm supplies FCU and medial FDP. Elbow entrapment at the cubital tunnel weakens ulnar-side flexion and can cause paresthesia in the ulnar digits; detailed sensory findings are board/clinical enrichment.

LesionWhereDeficit and discriminator
Pronator syndromeMedian compression near/between pronator teres headsForearm pain and median-pattern paresthesias; proximal distribution differs from isolated carpal tunnel (clinical enrichment)
AIN syndromeMedian motor branch in forearmWeak FPL + lateral FDP → impaired OK sign; no cutaneous sensory loss (clinical enrichment)
Cubital tunnel syndromeUlnar nerve around medial elbowUlnar digit sensory symptoms; weak FCU and digit 4–5 DIP flexion, potentially intrinsic hand weakness (clinical enrichment)
Carpal tunnel syndromeMedian nerve at wrist beneath flexor retinaculumDistal median symptoms; forearm flexors usually spared (clinical enrichment)
FIRST AID CONNECTION

High-value distinction: AIN palsy is purely motor; cubital tunnel is usually a mixed ulnar neuropathy with sensory complaints; pronator syndrome is more proximal than carpal tunnel. These diagnostic distinctions extend the professor’s course illustrations.

Retrieval checkpoint · Why does isolated AIN syndrome affect the OK sign without numbness?

AIN provides motor innervation to FPL, PQ and lateral FDP but no cutaneous sensory branch.

Objectives 5 and 7

Vessels, lymphatics, and image identification

Arterial branching

Brachial artery → radial + ulnar arteries. The ulnar artery gives ulnar recurrent branches and the common interosseous, which splits into anterior/posterior interosseous arteries. The radial artery gives a radial recurrent branch. Recurrent and collateral vessels provide alternate flow routes around a flexed elbow. The named recurrent branches are taught directly; the functional description of the anastomosis is anatomical/clinical enrichment because the slides do not map all collateral connections.

Veins, lymphatics and pulses

  • Cephalic vein: lateral superficial forearm; basilic vein: medial superficial forearm. The lecture depicts dorsal venous network and superficial hand venous arches.
  • Hand lymphatic plexus → superficial lymphatic vessels → axillary/apical nodes (slide 43).
  • Pulse sites: radial pulse on anterior lateral wrist; brachial pulse medial to biceps tendon at elbow (clinical application, not explicitly described on these slides).

Radiographic practical recognition

Use the anterior/AP and lateral X-ray comparisons to identify radial and ulnar styloids, radial tuberosity, radial head, capitulum, trochlea, trochlear notch and olecranon. The TFCC MRI on slide 10 is the lecture’s clearest MRI landmark; detailed CT interpretation is not provided by these slides.

PRACTICAL IMAGE

Unlabeled follow-up: On an AP elbow, which side is radial/lateral? Which rounded distal-humeral articular surface contacts the radial head? On the lateral elbow, locate the posterior olecranon.

Retrieval checkpoint · Which artery gives rise to the common interosseous artery? Which superficial vein is lateral?

Ulnar artery; cephalic vein.

Wrap-up

Master these before moving on

  1. Layer logic: 4 superficial, 1 intermediate, 3 deep. Predict locations from forearm cross sections.
  2. Innervation exception: median supplies all but FCU and medial FDP; AIN innervates deep radial flexors/pronator.
  3. Attachment → motion: middle phalanx = PIP flexion; distal phalanx = DIP or thumb IP flexion.
  4. Joint mechanics: capitulum/radial head, trochlea/ulna, annular ligament for radial head, TFCC distally.
  5. Vascular tree: brachial to radial and ulnar, then recurrent/interosseous branches.

Most useful First Aid connections

AIN palsy → impaired OK sign without cutaneous numbness; proximal median entrapment versus carpal tunnel; ulnar injury at elbow → FCU/medial FDP deficits; FOOSH → distal radius fracture; annular ligament traction → nursemaid’s elbow.
